failures.message: The evidence base cannot answer the central question.
failures.offending: The evidence base lacks the material needed to argue the counterfactual either way. (1) No evidence establishes what a timely, accurate warning could realistically have achieved in 1900 Galveston — there is nothing on evacuation capacity, train/ferry schedules, bridge throughput, lead times required, or how residents responded to warnings in comparable storms, so 'could the city have been saved' cannot be assessed. (2) The evidence never states when Gangoite/Belén concluded the storm was bound for Texas relative to the Bureau's Sept 7 realization (e102), so the claimed forecast advantage cannot be quantified. (3) No evidence says whether Belén's forecast, even if not blocked, would have reached Galveston or been acted upon — nothing on how Cuban reports entered the U.S. warning chain, whether Moore's blockade (e14) actually suppressed specific Texas-relevant warnings, or whether the Bureau would have accepted them given its dismissal of Cuban forecasters (e13, e437). (4) No evidence attributes any portion of the death toll to the wrong-track forecast versus other causes (complacency e191, Cline's 1891 article e24-e25, the word 'hurricane' ban e23, late warning e452) — e29 attributes loss of life to Galveston officials brushing off reports, which cuts against the forecast-blame thesis and is left unreconciled. (5) Nothing estimates deaths preventable by earlier warning (e.g., how many of the 6,000–12,000 died before any warning was possible on Sept 8, given flooding began early morning, e172). (6) No counterfactual scholarship or historian's assessment on this specific question is included.
